analysis.answer: Current law punishes assault as a misdemeanor with up to one year in jail. The measure creates a specific felony offense for assaulting an on-duty law enforcement officer and increases the maximum penalty to three years in prison.

Increasing the maximum sentence length and shifting sentences from county jails to state prisons will likely increase state incarceration costs. Felony prosecutions also typically consume more court and public defense resources than misdemeanors.

Taxpayers bear the increased costs of state incarceration and felony trials. Law enforcement officers may benefit from increased deterrence or longer incapacitation of those who assault them. Individuals convicted of the offense bear the cost of longer sentences and the lifelong collateral consequences of a felony record.
Prosecutors gain more leverage in plea negotiations by having a higher felony charge available, potentially securing longer sentences or extracting guilty pleas to lesser charges.

The measure addresses the perceived inadequacy of misdemeanor penalties for assaulting law enforcement officers. By increasing the maximum sentence and making it a felony, it aims to increase deterrence and provide harsher punishment.
Prosecutors gain greater discretion and leverage in charging and plea bargaining by having a more severe felony charge available for assaults involving officers.

Researchers dispute the deterrent effect of increasing sentence lengths. Some studies suggest longer sentences deter future crime and incapacitate offenders, while others find that the certainty of being caught deters crime more effectively than the severity of the punishment, and that longer prison terms can actually increase recidivism.
